title: 6.10 — Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS)
breadcrumb: Unit VI → Regression and linear models → 6.10 Two-stage least squares
engineName: Build the first stage, form fitted endogenous regressors and understand the 2SLS projection estimator.
objectives: Explain why 2SLS is used when structural regressors are endogenous.
Construct the instrument matrix from included exogenous regressors and excluded instruments.
Estimate the first-stage regression and interpret fitted endogenous regressors.
Describe the second stage and distinguish it from a naive two-step standard-error calculation.
Write the matrix 2SLS estimator using the projection matrix P_Z.
Recognise identification, weak-instrument and overidentification issues in a 2SLS design.

prereq.name: Endogeneity and instrumental variables
prereq.why: 2SLS uses valid instruments to isolate exogenous variation in endogenous regressors.

prereq.name: Matrix OLS and projection matrices
prereq.why: The 2SLS formula uses the projection onto the instrument space.

prereq.name: Linear regression and fitted values
prereq.why: The two stages are ordinary least-squares projections with a different regressor set.

traps: The instrument matrix contains all exogenous regressors, including included exogenous controls and excluded instruments.
The first stage regresses each endogenous RHS variable on the full instrument set.
The second stage regresses Y on included exogenous controls and fitted endogenous regressors.
Fitted values are generated by projecting endogenous regressors onto the instrument space.
The matrix estimator is (X′P_ZX)⁻¹X′P_ZY, with P_Z=Z(Z′Z)⁻¹Z′ when Z has full column rank.
A naive OLS standard error from treating fitted values as observed regressors is generally wrong; use the 2SLS covariance estimator.
With one endogenous regressor and one excluded instrument, 2SLS equals the just-identified IV/Wald ratio.
2SLS does not cure invalid instruments or weak relevance.
howto: List the endogenous regressors and all exogenous variables. Build Z from every included exogenous regressor plus every excluded instrument. Regress each endogenous regressor on Z to obtain fitted values. Regress Y on the included exogenous controls and those fitted values. Interpret the coefficient as 2SLS and use the proper 2SLS covariance estimator rather than naive second-stage OLS standard errors.

sheet: 2SLS estimates structural coefficients when some RHS regressors are endogenous and valid instruments are available.
The instrument matrix Z contains all included exogenous regressors plus excluded instruments.
First stage: regress each endogenous RHS variable on the full Z matrix.
Use fitted endogenous values from the first stage in the structural second stage.
Second stage: regress Y on included exogenous controls and fitted endogenous regressors.
P_Z=Z(Z′Z)⁻¹Z′ is the projection onto the instrument space.
With one endogenous regressor and one excluded instrument, 2SLS equals the just-identified IV ratio.
Do not use naive second-stage OLS standard errors that ignore generated regressors.
2SLS still requires relevant, valid instruments and sufficient rank.
cards: Y on included exogenous controls + fitted endogenous regressors
tricks: Do not omit included exogenous controls from the instrument matrix.
Every endogenous RHS variable gets its own first-stage regression on the full instrument set.
The second-stage point estimate is obtained using fitted values, but its standard errors need the 2SLS formula.
A strong first stage does not prove the exclusion restriction.
shortcuts: First stage predicts X; second stage estimates Y using predicted X.
P_Z projects onto the space spanned by all exogenous instruments.
One endogenous variable plus one valid excluded instrument gives the Wald ratio.
remember: 2SLS is a single estimator with a two-stage computational representation; do not treat the second-stage OLS standard errors as final.
If instruments are weak or invalid, the 2SLS estimator can be unreliable even when the steps are executed correctly.

scenes.title: Refresh OLS projections and IV conditions
scenes.objective: Recover the concepts needed to understand the two stages.
body: 2SLS replaces an endogenous regressor by the part of it explained by exogenous instruments. It is therefore built from ordinary least-squares projections, but it is not ordinary least squares on the original endogenous regressor.
Before following the two stages, recall the instrument conditions and the geometry of fitted values.

items.ask: What does a fitted value from OLS represent?
items.recall: The projection of the observed response or regressor onto the span of the included regressors.
refresh: OLS fitted values are linear combinations of the columns in the design matrix.
In matrix notation, fitted values are P_X y, where P_X is the projection onto the column space of X.
2SLS uses the same idea to project endogenous regressors onto the instrument space.
Relevance means the instrument predicts the endogenous regressor after conditioning on included controls.
Exclusion means the instrument has no direct route to the structural outcome and is uncorrelated with the structural disturbance conditional on controls.
2SLS cannot repair an instrument that violates either identifying requirement.

items.ask: What is the role of included exogenous controls?
items.recall: They remain in the structural equation and are also instruments for themselves.
refresh: The instrument matrix includes all exogenous variables in the model, not only the excluded instruments.
Included exogenous controls appear directly in the second-stage structural regression and in the first-stage instrument set.
Leaving them out of Z changes the estimator and can destroy the intended orthogonality conditions.

ask.q: What is projected in the first stage of 2SLS?
ask.nudge: It is the endogenous right-hand-side regressor, not the outcome.

scenes.title: Replace endogenous variation with instrument-predicted variation
scenes.objective: Build an intuitive picture of the first and second stages.
body: Suppose observed education is endogenous because ability affects both schooling and earnings. A valid instrument predicts part of schooling but is assumed not to carry the omitted ability component into earnings.
The first stage isolates the component of schooling explained by the instrument and exogenous controls. The second stage relates earnings to that predicted schooling component.
The method does not discard all observed schooling information; it uses the part that is linearly explained by the exogenous instrument set.

scenario.teaser: Schooling predicted by a policy instrument
scenario.title: The two-stage idea
body: An analyst wants the effect of education on earnings, but education is endogenous. A policy instrument and background controls are available.
In the first stage, education is regressed on the policy instrument and all included exogenous controls. The fitted value is the part of schooling predicted by that exogenous information.

In the second stage, earnings are regressed on the fitted education value and the included exogenous controls. This removes the endogenous component of schooling from the identifying variation used for the slope.
The instrument still needs a relevance and exclusion argument. The two-stage calculation is not a substitute for defending the design.
scenario.q: What does the fitted schooling value retain?
scenario.answer: The component of schooling linearly predicted by the full exogenous instrument set.

ask.q: Why not use the original observed education variable in the second stage?
ask.nudge: It contains the endogenous variation that made OLS inconsistent.

scenes.title: The instrument matrix and first stage
scenes.objective: Construct Z correctly and obtain fitted endogenous regressors.

blocks.body: Let X contain all structural regressors, including endogenous and exogenous variables. Let Z contain every exogenous variable in the system: included exogenous controls plus excluded instruments.
For each endogenous column x_j, regress x_j on the full Z matrix. The fitted column is x̂_j=P_Zx_j, where P_Z=Z(Z′Z)⁻¹Z′ if Z has full column rank.
An exogenous control that appears in the structural equation is included in Z as well. The first stage must not omit it merely because it is not an excluded instrument.
If several structural regressors are endogenous, each is projected on the same full instrument matrix. Identification requires enough independent excluded instruments and the relevant rank condition.

nodes.label: Regress each endogenous X on Z
Regress Y on controls and X̂

ask.nudge: Include the excluded instruments and every included exogenous control.

scenes.problem: For Z values −1, 0, 1, the observed endogenous regressor is X=(1,2,4) and the outcome is Y=(2,5,8). Compute the first-stage and reduced-form slopes and the just-identified 2SLS slope.

steps.say: The means are X̄=7/3, Ȳ=5 and Z̄=0.
steps.why: The centred instrument sum of squares is two.
This is the change in X per unit change in Z.
This is the change in Y per unit change in Z.
In the just-identified case the 2SLS estimate equals reduced form divided by first stage.

ask.q: Why does the ratio give the structural slope in this just-identified example?
ask.nudge: The instrument's outcome effect equals the structural slope times its first-stage effect.

scenes.title: Recall the two-stage sequence
scenes.objective: Retrieve the exact roles of the two stages.
scenes.intro: Answer from memory before reading the explanation.

items.q: What is regressed in the first stage?
items.a: Each endogenous structural regressor is regressed on the full instrument matrix Z.
All included exogenous controls and all excluded instruments.

items.q: What is used in the second stage?
items.a: The outcome is regressed on the included exogenous controls and the fitted endogenous regressors.

scenes.problem: Fill in the pieces of the projection-based estimator.

steps.say: The instrument projection matrix is formed from Z.

blank.hint: The matrix on the right transposes the instrument matrix.

steps.say: Project the endogenous regressors onto the instrument space.

blank.hint: Apply the projection matrix to X.
The right-hand side projects Y through the instrument space.

blank.prompt: Do not report naive second-stage OLS standard _____.
blank.hint: The fitted regressors are generated in the first stage.

scenes.title: Second stage and matrix estimator
scenes.objective: Connect the computational steps to the 2SLS estimator.

blocks.body: β̂_2SLS=(X′P_ZX)⁻¹X′P_ZY, where P_Z=Z(Z′Z)⁻¹Z′. Equivalently, use the projected endogenous columns P_ZX together with included exogenous regressors.
The first stage produces the fitted endogenous regressors P_ZX. The second-stage cross-products with those fitted values yield X′P_ZX and X′P_ZY.

The second-stage OLS point estimate is a convenient computational representation, but its naive OLS covariance formula treats fitted regressors as fixed observed data. Use the 2SLS covariance estimator based on the original X and instrument matrix.

With one endogenous regressor and one excluded instrument, the 2SLS coefficient equals the Wald ratio of the reduced-form to first-stage coefficient. With more instruments, the projection combines information across the instrument space.

ask.q: Why are naive second-stage OLS standard errors generally inappropriate?
ask.nudge: The fitted endogenous regressors were estimated, not directly observed.

scenes.title: What 2SLS does not repair
scenes.objective: Distinguish a correct algorithm from a valid identifying design.
body: 2SLS is a way to use exogenous variation in endogenous regressors. It does not turn an invalid instrument into a valid one, and it cannot manufacture first-stage strength when the instrument barely predicts the endogenous variable.
A correctly executed second stage can still be biased or imprecise if exclusion fails or instruments are weak. The quality of the design remains central.

scenario.teaser: A correctly run model with weak instruments
scenario.title: Good computation, weak identification
body: An analyst constructs Z correctly, runs all first stages and computes the 2SLS matrix estimator. The excluded instruments have very small partial first-stage relationships with the endogenous regressors.

The algebra and software implementation may be correct, but the identifying variation is weak. The estimator can be highly variable and conventional asymptotic approximations may be poor in finite samples.
If an instrument also affects the outcome directly, the problem is more serious: exclusion fails, and 2SLS is inconsistent even if the first stage is strong.
The correct conclusion is to assess instrument strength and validity separately, report suitable inference and revisit the research design.
scenario.q: Does correct 2SLS computation guarantee a credible causal estimate?
scenario.answer: No. Instrument relevance, exclusion and rank must still hold.

ask.q: Which issue cannot be fixed by following the 2SLS steps correctly?
ask.nudge: The estimator depends on assumptions about the instruments, not only on computation.

scenes.title: Worked example: identify the full instrument set
scenes.objective: Construct the instrument matrix for a structural equation.
scenes.problem: The structural equation is Y=β₀+β₁X+β₂W+u. X is endogenous; W is exogenous and included. Z₁ and Z₂ are excluded instruments. What belongs in the instrument matrix?

steps.why: W is included and exogenous; Z₁ and Z₂ are excluded instruments.

steps.say: Do not leave W out merely because it is included in the structural equation.
steps.why: The intercept is also included when the model has one.

steps.say: The first stage predicts X using the full Z.
steps.why: The fitted X contains the component explained by all exogenous information.

steps.say: The second stage keeps W and replaces X with X̂.
steps.why: Included exogenous controls remain in the structural equation.

ask.q: Why is W included in Z even though it is not excluded?

scenes.title: Guided problem: detect a missing control in Z
scenes.objective: Diagnose an incorrectly specified first stage.
scenes.problem: The structural equation includes exogenous control W and endogenous regressor X. The analyst regresses X only on excluded instruments Z₁ and Z₂, omitting W. What is wrong?
hints: List all exogenous variables in the structural equation.
Recall which variables belong in the full instrument matrix.
Explain why the first stage must include W.
scenes.answer: The first stage is misspecified for the intended 2SLS calculation because the full instrument matrix must include W as well as Z₁ and Z₂.

solution.say: W is exogenous and included in the structural equation.
solution.math: W ∈ X and W is exogenous

solution.say: Every included exogenous regressor belongs in Z.
Omitting W changes the instrument space and first-stage projection.
solution.math: P_ZX is computed from the full Z

solution.say: The correct second stage retains W and uses fitted X.

ask.q: Which variable was incorrectly omitted from the instrument matrix?
ask.nudge: It is an included exogenous control.

scenes.title: Exam traps: first stage, second stage and inference
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false.

items.claim: The first stage regresses each endogenous RHS variable on the full exogenous instrument set.
items.why: The instrument matrix includes included controls and excluded instruments.

items.claim: Included exogenous controls are omitted from Z because they are not excluded instruments.
items.why: Included exogenous regressors instrument themselves and belong in Z.

items.claim: The second stage uses fitted endogenous regressors and included exogenous controls.
items.why: This is the computational representation of 2SLS.

items.claim: Naive second-stage OLS standard errors are generally the final 2SLS standard errors.
items.why: The covariance estimator must account for the first-stage projection.

items.claim: 2SLS can be inconsistent when exclusion fails.
items.why: The estimator still relies on valid instrument moment conditions.

scenes.title: Transfer problem: choose the correct inference
scenes.objective: Select the correct standard-error approach after 2SLS.
scenes.problem: A researcher obtains the 2SLS coefficient by regressing Y on X̂ and controls in the second stage. The software reports ordinary OLS standard errors from that regression. What should be reported?
hints: Separate the point-estimation computation from its covariance formula.
Remember that X̂ is a generated regressor.
Use the original structural X and instrument matrix in the 2SLS covariance calculation.
scenes.answer: Use the proper 2SLS covariance estimator (and robust or clustered variants if justified), not naive second-stage OLS standard errors.

solution.say: The second-stage coefficient may reproduce the 2SLS point estimate.
The fitted regressors are estimated projections.
Naive OLS covariance treats X̂ as fixed observed data.

ask.q: What is wrong with treating the second-stage OLS standard errors as final?
ask.nudge: They ignore how the fitted regressors were constructed.

scenes.title: Summary: predict, replace, estimate and infer
scenes.objective: Compress the 2SLS procedure into an exam-ready sequence.
body: Build Z from every included exogenous regressor and every excluded instrument. Regress each endogenous RHS variable on Z and retain its fitted value P_ZX.
The second stage regresses Y on included exogenous controls and fitted endogenous regressors. In matrix form, β̂_2SLS=(X′P_ZX)⁻¹X′P_ZY.

The two-stage representation gives the coefficient estimate, but naive second-stage OLS standard errors are generally not the correct 2SLS inference. Use the 2SLS covariance formula and remember that relevance, exclusion and rank remain necessary.

ask.nudge: Build Z, estimate the first stage, fit X and estimate the second stage.

scenes.title: Extension — 2SLS as a projection estimator
scenes.objective: Derive the projection form and its homoscedastic covariance.

blocks.body: P_Z=Z(Z′Z)⁻¹Z′ is symmetric and idempotent when Z has full column rank. It projects any vector onto the column space spanned by the instruments.
The 2SLS estimator is β̂=(X′P_ZX)⁻¹X′P_ZY. If the structural disturbance has variance σ²I, the conventional covariance is σ²(X′P_ZX)⁻¹.
With heteroscedasticity or clustering, replace the conventional covariance with an appropriate sandwich estimator. The point-estimation projection is unchanged.
